About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“The Master said: Is it not a pleasure to learn and to practice what one has learned in due time? Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar? Is it not the mark of a gentleman to remain unresentful when others fail to appreciate one?”
Classical Chinese
“學而時習之，不亦說乎？有朋自遠方來，不亦樂乎？人不知而不慍，不亦君子乎？”

Three rhetorical questions opening the Analects. The archive's rendering expands each into English clause order; the Chinese is far more compact.

Attribution notes

The first line of the Analects (1.1), and therefore the most-quoted sentence in the Confucian corpus and the one most often detached from it. The three questions form a sequence that later commentary treats as a progression — learning alone, learning shared, learning unrecognised — so quoting only the first (“Is it not a pleasure to learn…”) drops the two stages that follow.

About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

How to read this passage

Education is not only information transfer; it is the shaping of attention and character. Confucian learning, Socratic midwifery, and Deweyan growth offer rival models. This passage enters that discussion through learning.
